Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

2. Command Execution:

   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

# `csv` module: Exact Statements from the Documentation

Some requested topics are not covered on this page. Those are marked **Not stated on this page**.

## `newline=''` requirement

From `reader()` and `writer()`:

> If _csvfile_ is a file object, it should be opened with `newline=''`.

From footnote [1]:

> If `newline=''` is not specified, newlines embedded inside quoted fields will not be interpreted correctly, and on platforms that use `\r\n` line endings on write an extra `\r` will be added. It should always be safe to specify `newline=''`, since the csv module does its own (universal) newline handling.

```python
with open('eggs.csv', newline='') as csvfile:
    reader = csv.reader(csvfile)
```

## `line_num` semantics

> The number of lines read from the source iterator. This is not the same as the number of records returned, as records can span multiple lines.

It counts physical lines read from the source, not records. The page's error-reporting example uses it:

```python
sys.exit(f'file {filename}, line {reader.line_num}: {e}')
```

## Blank line behavior (empty list)

**Not stated on this page.** The only related wording is in `DictReader`, which refers to "a non-blank row" when describing missing fields. The page does not say what `reader` returns for a blank line.

## `utf-8-sig`

**Not mentioned on this page.** The page only says:

> Since `open()` is used to open a CSV file for reading, the file will by default be decoded into Unicode using UTF-8. To decode a file using a different encoding, use the `encoding` argument of open:

```python
with open('some.csv', newline='', encoding='latin-1') as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
```

## `strict` mode

From the `Dialect` attributes:

> `Dialect.strict`: When `True`, raise exception `Error` on bad CSV input. The default is `False`.

## `field_size_limit`

> `csv.field_size_limit()`: Returns the current maximum field size allowed by the parser. If _new_limit_ is given, this becomes the new limit.

The page does not state the default value.

## `lineterminator` (writer)

> `Dialect.lineterminator`: The string used to terminate lines produced by the `writer`. It defaults to `'\r\n'`.

Reader behavior is separate:

> The `reader` is hard-coded to recognise either `'\r'` or `'\n'` as end-of-line, and ignores _lineterminator_. This behavior may change in the future.

## `QUOTE_MINIMAL`

> Instructs `writer` objects to only quote those fields which contain special characters such as _delimiter_, _quotechar_, `'\r'`, `'\n'` or any of the characters in _lineterminator_. If _doublequote_ is `False` and _escapechar_ is set, the _quotechar_ is escaped instead of causing the field to be quoted.

`QUOTE_MINIMAL` is the default when `quotechar` is not `None`.

## `Error` exceptions

> `exception csv.Error`: Raised by any of the functions when an error is detected.

The page also specifies these cases:

- `unregister_dialect(name)` and `get_dialect(name)`: "An `Error` is raised if _name_ is not a registered dialect name."
- `QUOTE_NONE` writing: "If _escapechar_ is not set, the writer will raise `Error` if any characters that require escaping are encountered."
- `doublequote=False` writing: "if _doublequote_ is `False` and no _escapechar_ is set, `Error` is raised if a _quotechar_ is found in a field."

The provided page content is truncated before `str.strip()` and `str.splitlines()`, so I can't quote their documentation. The `casefold`, `lower`, and digit-method sections are included.

**str.strip() whitespace definition:** Not in the provided content.

**str.splitlines separators:** Not in the provided content.

**str.casefold() vs. str.lower()**

> Casefolding is similar to lowercasing but more aggressive because it is intended to remove all case distinctions in a string. For example, the German lowercase letter `'ß'` is equivalent to `"ss"`. Since it is already lowercase, [`lower()`] would do nothing to `'ß'`; `casefold()` converts it to `"ss"`.

```python
>>> 'straße'.lower()
'straße'
>>> 'straße'.casefold()
'strasse'
```

The page also says: "Casefolded strings may be used for caseless matching." The casefolding algorithm is described in section 3.13.3 "Default Case Folding" of the Unicode Standard. The method was added in Python 3.3.

**str.isdecimal(), str.isdigit(), str.isnumeric()**

- **`isdecimal()`**: "Decimal characters are those that can be used to form numbers in base 10, such as U+0660, ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT ZERO. Formally a decimal character is a character in the Unicode General Category 'Nd'."
- **`isdigit()`**: "Digits include decimal characters and digits that need special handling, such as the compatibility superscript digits... Formally, a digit is a character that has the property value Numeric_Type=Digit or Numeric_Type=Decimal."
- **`isnumeric()`**: "Numeric characters include digit characters, and all characters that have the Unicode numeric value property, e.g. U+2155, VULGAR FRACTION ONE FIFTH. Formally, numeric characters are those with the property value Numeric_Type=Digit, Numeric_Type=Decimal or Numeric_Type=Numeric."

The page's examples show the difference:

```python
>>> '²'.isdecimal(), '²'.isdigit(),  '²'.isnumeric()
(False, True, True)
>>> '⅕'.isdigit()   # Vulgar fraction one fifth
False
>>> '⅕'.isnumeric()
True
```

So superscript digits such as `²` are digits and numeric but not decimal, and `⅕` is numeric but neither decimal nor digit.

## utf-8-sig decoding

From the `encodings.utf_8_sig` section:

> "This module implements a variant of the UTF-8 codec. On encoding, a UTF-8 encoded BOM will be prepended to the UTF-8 encoded bytes. For the stateful encoder this is only done once (on the first write to the byte stream). On decoding, an optional UTF-8 encoded BOM at the start of the data will be skipped."

From the Encodings and Unicode section:

> "On decoding `utf-8-sig` will skip those three bytes if they appear as the first three bytes in the file."

- The BOM is skipped only when present ("optional"), and only at the start of the data.
- The page does not use the word "once" for decoding. That behavior is implied by "at the start," since only the leading three bytes are skipped.

## Error handlers

From the Error Handlers section, the `'strict'` row:

> "Raise [UnicodeError] (or a subclass), this is the default. Implemented in `strict_errors()`."

From `codecs.strict_errors(exception)`:

> "Each encoding or decoding error raises a UnicodeError."

From `codecs.decode()`:

> "The default error handler is `'strict'` meaning that decoding errors raise ValueError (or a more codec specific subclass, such as UnicodeDecodeError)."

The page does not state the exception type for `utf-8-sig` specifically. It documents the general `'strict'` behavior, and `UnicodeDecodeError` is given as the codec-specific example.

## UTF-8 decoding of a BOM

From the Encodings and Unicode section:

> "As UTF-8 is an 8-bit encoding no BOM is required and any `U+FEFF` character in the decoded string (even if it's the first character) is treated as a `ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE`."

> "In UTF-8, the use of the BOM is discouraged and should generally be avoided."

So plain `utf-8` does not strip a leading BOM. It decodes to `U+FEFF`. Only `utf-8-sig` skips it.

## open() error handling

The page does not document the `errors` parameter of the built-in `open()`. It only says:

> "While the builtin `open()` and the associated `io` module are the recommended approach for working with encoded text files, this module provides additional utility functions..."

For the deprecated `codecs.open()`:

> "_errors_ may be given to define the error handling. It defaults to `'strict'` which causes a `ValueError` to be raised in case an encoding error occurs."

> "Deprecated since version 3.14: `codecs.open()` has been superseded by `open()`."

Also relevant to `codecs.open()`:

> "If _encoding_ is not `None`, then the underlying encoded files are always opened in binary mode. No automatic conversion of `'\n'` is done on reading and writing."

For `open()` error details, consult the `io` / built-in `open()` documentation, which is not part of this page.

## `\d` (decimal digits)

- **str patterns:** "Matches any Unicode decimal digit (that is, any character in Unicode character category [Nd]). This includes `[0-9]`, and also many other digit characters. Matches `[0-9]` if the `ASCII` flag is used."
- **bytes patterns:** "Matches any decimal digit in the ASCII character set; this is equivalent to `[0-9]`."
- **`\D`:** "Matches any character which is not a decimal digit. This is the opposite of `\d`. Matches `[^0-9]` if the `ASCII` flag is used."

## `re.ASCII` flag

"Make `\w`, `\W`, `\b`, `\B`, `\d`, `\D`, `\s` and `\S` perform ASCII-only matching instead of full Unicode matching. This is only meaningful for Unicode (str) patterns, and is ignored for bytes patterns. Corresponds to the inline flag `(?a)`."

The page also notes that `re.U`/`re.UNICODE` is redundant in Python 3, since str patterns match Unicode by default.

## `$` (end of string)

"Matches the end of the string or just before the newline at the end of the string, and in `MULTILINE` mode also matches before a newline. `foo` matches both 'foo' and 'foobar', while the regular expression `foo$` matches only 'foo'. ... searching for a single `$` in `'foo\n'` will find two (empty) matches: one just before the newline, and one at the end of the string."

```python
re.fullmatch(r"foo", "foo\n")   # None
re.search(r"foo$", "foo\n")     # matches 'foo' (before the trailing newline)
```

## `\Z` and `\z` (3.14)

- **`\z`:** "Matches only at the end of the string. Added in version 3.14."
- **`\Z`:** "The same as `\z`. For compatibility with old Python versions."

On versions before 3.14, use `\Z`. The page does not describe any other behavioral difference between the two.

## `re.fullmatch`

"If the whole _string_ matches the regular expression _pattern_, return a corresponding `Match`. Return `None` if the string does not match the pattern; note that this is different from a zero-length match." (Added in version 3.4.)


- `round()` ignores the context rounding when no ndigits is given: "rounding ties to even, and ignoring the rounding mode of the `Decimal` context."
  ```python
  >>> getcontext().rounding = ROUND_DOWN
  >>> round(Decimal('3.75'))     # context rounding ignored

  >>> round(Decimal('3.75'), 0)  # uses the context rounding
  Decimal('3')
  ```

## Negative zero

- "The standard also differentiates `-0` from `+0`."
- "The signed zeros can result from calculations that underflow... Since their magnitude is zero, both positive and negative zeros are treated as equal and their sign is informational."
- `is_signed()`: "Note that zeros and NaNs can both carry signs."
- The page does not show `Decimal('-0.00')` output or its `str()` form directly.

## Equality and hash of Decimal('1.0') vs Decimal('1.00')

- The page does not explicitly document hash behavior.
- Numeric equality is implied by the FAQ: "The numbers `200`, `200.000`, `2E2`, and `.02E+4` all have the same value at various precisions."

- To remove the exponent, the FAQ uses:

  ```python
  def remove_exponent(d):

  >>> remove_exponent(Decimal('5E+3'))
  Decimal('5000')
  ```
- `capitals`: "If set to `1`, exponents are printed with a capital `E`; otherwise, a lowercase `e` is used." The default is `1`.
- `to_eng_string()`: "Engineering notation has an exponent which is a multiple of 3."

- "Unlike other operations, if the length of the coefficient after the quantize operation would be greater than precision, then an InvalidOperation is signaled. This guarantees that, unless there is an error condition, the quantized exponent is always equal to that of the right-hand operand."
- `round(number, ndigits)` raises InvalidOperation "if the length of the coefficient after the quantize operation would be greater than the current context's precision."
- Validation pattern from the FAQ:
  ```python
  >>> Decimal('3.214').quantize(TWOPLACES, context=Context(traps=[Inexact]))
  Traceback (most recent call last):
     ...
  Inexact: None
  ```
- Constructor limits: "If the internal limits of the C version are exceeded, constructing a decimal raises InvalidOperation."
- DefaultContext enables traps for "Overflow, InvalidOperation, and DivisionByZero."

  ```
  nan      ::=  'NaN' [digits] | 'sNaN' [digits]
  ```
- "Case is not significant, so, for example, `inf`, `Inf`, `INFINITY`, and `iNfINity` are all acceptable spellings for positive infinity."
- `Decimal('NaN')` and `Decimal('-Infinity')` are valid constructions.

- "Note that rounding is applied *before* reducing to simplest form."
- FAQ example:
  ```python
  >>> values = map(Decimal, '200 200.000 2E2 .02E+4'.split())
  >>> [v.normalize() for v in values]
  [Decimal('2E+2'), Decimal('2E+2'), Decimal('2E+2'), Decimal('2E+2')]
  ```
- "In the latest versions of the specification, this operation is also known as `reduce`."

# Research report: Python 3.11+ pitfalls for byte-deterministic `csvledger`

I fetched the official docs for csv, decimal, re, stdtypes and codecs. WebSearch was not needed. I did not run any code. Items marked **[unverified]** are not stated on the fetched doc pages. They come from my knowledge of CPython and should be confirmed with a quick `python -I` check before the spec freezes them. No codebase files were relevant; the repo only has the seed commit.

## Key findings

1. **`newline=''` is mandatory when reading.** The docs say csv-reader files "should be opened with `newline=''`". Without it, newlines inside quoted fields are misread. On write, platforms that use `\r\n` get an extra `\r`. The reader recognises `\r` and `\n` itself and ignores `lineterminator`.
2. **`utf-8-sig` skips a BOM only at the start.** Decoding with `utf-8-sig` skips an optional leading BOM. Plain `utf-8` keeps it as U+FEFF. Plain `utf-8` therefore leaves `\ufeff` glued to the first header name, which breaks column matching. The docs describe no multi-BOM handling, so a second BOM would stay in the data.
3. **`line_num` counts physical lines, not records.** The docs say it is "the number of lines read from the source iterator… not the same as the number of records returned". A multiline quoted field advances it by more than 1 per record. After a record is returned, `line_num` is the line where that record ends, not where it starts. For the start line, record `line_num` before each `next()` and add 1 **[unverified]**. Error messages that cite `line_num` are only deterministic if the spec defines which line they mean.
4. **Blank lines and zero-field rows are undocumented.** The csv page does not say what the reader returns for a blank line. CPython yields `[]` for an empty line. A line holding only whitespace yields `['   ']`, and `""` yields `['']` **[unverified]**. So the spec must say how it treats `[]`, a single empty field, and a whitespace-only field. `csv.Error` is the reader's exception; it is raised on bad input only in `strict` mode (default off) or for field-size overflow. The default field size limit is 131072 **[unverified]**.
5. **`quantize` rounds with the context, not the argument.** The default context rounding is `ROUND_HALF_EVEN`, so `ROUND_HALF_UP` ("ties going away from zero") must be passed explicitly: `d.quantize(Q, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)`. `round(d)` and `format(d, '.2f')` follow other rules. The docs show `.2f` obeying the context rounding, and `round()` with no ndigits ignores it and uses half-even.
6. **`quantize` can raise `InvalidOperation`.** It signals this if the result's coefficient would exceed the context precision (default 28 digits). Huge amounts therefore raise rather than round. The spec needs a bounded-magnitude rule and a deterministic error for this case.
7. **Negative zero exists and prints with a sign.** The docs say `-0` and `+0` are distinct in representation but compare equal. A value like `Decimal('-0.004').quantize(Decimal('0.01'), ROUND_HALF_UP)` gives `Decimal('-0.00')`, and `str()` and `format(…, 'f')` print `-0.00` **[unverified]**. Rendering must normalize this, for example `if q.is_zero(): q = abs(q)`, or an equivalent `copy_abs`.
8. **Equal Decimals can differ in representation.** The docs show `Decimal('12.0').compare_total(Decimal('12'))` is `-1`, so representations differ even though `==` is true. The docs do not state hash behavior. Python's numeric hash invariant means equal values hash equal, so `Decimal('1.0')` and `Decimal('1.00')` collide as dict or set keys and `Decimal('-0') == Decimal('0')` **[unverified]**. For dedupe, key on the quantized value with the sign of zero removed. Also remember that `Decimal('NaN')` is never equal to itself, and `sNaN` raises on comparison.
9. **`str()` can produce exponent notation.** The docs say exponential notation is sometimes the only way to show significance, for example `Decimal('0E-1000026')`. `format(d, 'f')` never uses an exponent and is the safe choice. The docs show `format(Decimal('2.675'), 'f')` gives `'2.675'`. After quantizing to a fixed exponent, `format(q, 'f')` is stable. The `capitals` setting also affects the `E` case.
10. **`Decimal(str)` accepts far more than plain digits.** It strips leading and trailing whitespace and accepts underscores anywhere (3.6+). It also accepts any Unicode decimal digit, including Arabic-Indic and fullwidth, and it accepts `Infinity`, `Inf` and `NaN` in any case, plus `sNaN`. Raw `Decimal(field)` is therefore a validation hole. `Context.create_decimal()` rejects whitespace and underscores, but it still accepts Unicode digits and NaN. The safest approach is to validate with a strict regex first, then construct the Decimal.
11. **`\d` matches Unicode digits.** For str patterns it matches any Nd character, and `re.ASCII` or `[0-9]` restricts it to ASCII. The same applies to `\s`, `\w` and `\b`. Use `[0-9]` explicitly, or `re.ASCII`.
12. **`$` matches before a trailing newline.** `re.search(r'foo$', 'foo\n')` matches. `re.fullmatch` does not match `"foo\n"`, so it is the safe anchor. If you use `match` with an anchor, use `\Z`; `\z` exists only in 3.14+, so `\Z` is the portable form for 3.11 and later.
13. **`str.strip()` strips Unicode whitespace.** With no arguments it removes anything `str.isspace()` accepts. That includes NBSP U+00A0, U+2003 and U+3000, and also `\x1c` to `\x1f` and `\x85` **[unverified]**. U+FEFF (the BOM) and U+200B (zero-width space) are not whitespace, so they survive `strip()`. If the spec means ASCII-only trimming, it must call `strip(' \t')` or similar with explicit characters.
14. **`splitlines()` splits on more than `\n`.** The documented boundaries include `\v`, `\f`, `\x1c` to `\x1e`, `\x85`, `\u2028` and `\u2029`. It must not be used to split CSV or ledger text. Embedded U+2028 inside fields is legal data.
15. **`casefold()` is more aggressive than `lower()`.** The docs show `'straße'.casefold()` is `'strasse'`. It does not normalize composed versus decomposed forms, so `é` as one character differs from `e` plus a combining accent unless NFC or NFKC is applied first. Casefold is locale-independent. `lower()`, by contrast, leaves `ß` unchanged.
16. **Decode errors are `UnicodeDecodeError`.** The default `strict` handler raises it, and it is a `ValueError` subclass. In a lazy csv read it surfaces mid-iteration, after earlier rows were already processed, and not at `open()`. So output may be partial unless the program reads and validates everything before writing anything. `errors='replace'` would silently change data, which makes it unsuitable for a ledger.
17. **Platform-dependent defaults.** `open()` without `encoding=` uses the locale encoding (cp1252 on Windows) **[unverified]**. `csv.writer` defaults to `\r\n` line endings. `print` and `sys.stdout` text mode translates `\n` to `\r\n` on Windows **[unverified]**.

## Constraints the spec MUST respect

- Open input with `open(path, newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig')`. Always set `encoding` explicitly, and never rely on the locale.
- Write output bytes explicitly: open with `newline=''` and a fixed `lineterminator`. Alternatively write bytes to `sys.stdout.buffer`, because stdout text mode translates `\n` on Windows.
- Parse amounts with a strict ASCII regex, applied only after normalizing whitespace. Never pass raw field text to `Decimal()`.
- Use `fullmatch`, or `\Z` if anchoring. Never use a bare `$`.
- Round only with an explicit `ROUND_HALF_UP`, and render only with `format(q, 'f')`.
- Remove the sign from zero before rendering, so `-0.00` never appears.
- Reject NaN, sNaN and Infinity by not accepting them in the regex, and bound the magnitude so `quantize` cannot raise `InvalidOperation`.
- Dedupe on a canonical key, not on the raw Decimal or its string form.
- Define line-number semantics for errors, meaning whether they report physical lines, record numbers, or the start line of a record.
- Define behavior for blank rows (`[]`) and rows with the wrong field count.

## Recommendations for the spec

1. **Parsing.** Specify the amount grammar, for example `^[+-]?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]{1,N})?$` applied with `re.fullmatch` and no Unicode digits. State what happens with thousands separators, a leading `+`, `.5`, `5.`, and exponent forms like `1e3`, which should be rejected explicitly.
2. **Whitespace policy.** Pick one policy and name it, for example "trim only ASCII space and tab". Say whether NBSP or U+FEFF in a field is an error or is kept.
3. **Blank lines.** Skip fully empty rows (`[]`). State separately what a row of one empty field means, and say whether `[]` still consumes a `line_num`.
4. **Header handling.** Do the BOM strip through the `utf-8-sig` decoder only. Compare header names after a fixed normalization (strip, then `casefold`), and say whether NFC normalization is applied first.
5. **Dedupe key.** Use `(date, account, quantized_amount_str, ...)` with the zero sign removed. A string key from `format(q, 'f')` is deterministic and avoids relying on Decimal hash semantics.
6. **Errors.** Map `UnicodeDecodeError` and `csv.Error` to one documented exit code and message. Include the byte offset (`e.start`) or the record number and `line_num` consistently. Read the whole input before writing any output, so decode errors cannot leave partial output.
7. **Output.** Fix the line terminator (`\n` or `\r\n`), the quoting mode (`QUOTE_MINIMAL`) and the encoding (UTF-8 without BOM). Write through `newline=''` or `sys.stdout.buffer`, so Windows, macOS and Linux outputs match byte for byte.
8. **Sorting.** Do not rely on locale or on `lower()`. Sort on `casefold()` of NFC-normalized text, or on code points, and state the tie-break.
9. **Decimal context.** Use a local context with fixed precision and `ROUND_HALF_UP`, via `decimal.localcontext(Context(prec=P, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))`, so behavior doesn't depend on the thread's context.
10. **Tests.** Cover each of these:
    - a BOM-prefixed file
    - CRLF versus LF versus lone CR
    - a multiline quoted field
    - a blank line and a whitespace-only line
    - `-0.004`, `0.005`, `-0.005`, `1.0` versus `1.00`
    - fullwidth and Arabic-Indic digits
    - `NaN` and `Infinity`
    - a trailing newline inside a field with `$` anchoring
    - invalid UTF-8 bytes
    - a large magnitude that triggers `InvalidOperation`
    - NBSP padding

## Sources

- https://docs.python.org/3/library/csv.html
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/decimal.html
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html
- https://docs.python.org/3/library/codecs.html
